notes.title: CDT Unit 1 — ma'am's check-your-understanding questions
notes.content:
From the end of each chapter of ma'am's Unit I course notes (`course-notes/Unit_1_Notes_CDT.pdf`), with her model answers condensed. Her practice questions are the best guide to her exam.

1. **Name the four elements of computational thinking. (K1)**  
   Decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction, algorithm design.
2. **Explain, with an example, why technical skill alone is not enough. (K2)**  
   A technically excellent app fails if it ignores how people behave — e.g. an attendance app needing fast internet in classrooms with poor signal. Design thinking finds that need first.
3. **Apply all four elements to planning a college fest. (K3)**  
   Decomposition: venue, budget, events, publicity. Pattern: last year most registrations came in the final week. Abstraction: track only headcount and budget per event. Algorithm: a step-by-step plan for registration day.
4. **Define a problem using current and goal states. (K1)**  
   A gap between the current state and a desired goal state, where the path between them is not immediately obvious.
5. **Give three differences between well- and ill-structured problems. (K2)**  
   Any three: clarity of goal, availability of information, existence of a known method, number of correct answers.
6. **Break "improve student mental health on campus" into two better-structured sub-problems. (K3)**  
   "Reduce waiting time for a counselling appointment from three weeks to one"; "Raise students who know where to get help from 30% to 80% (survey)".
7. **Name the three groups of traits and one trait in each. (K1)**  
   Cognitive (curiosity), behavioural (persistence), collaborative (empathy).
8. **How does empathy improve technical problem-solving? (K2)**  
   You understand what users actually need, so you solve the real problem; it also improves teamwork.
9. **List the steps of Polya's method and of IDEAL. (K1)**  
   Polya: understand, plan, carry out, look back. IDEAL: identify, define, explore, act, look back.
10. **Why is IDEAL often better for ill-structured problems? (K2)**  
   It begins with identifying and defining the problem — exactly what is unclear in ill-structured problems.
11. **Polya: 240 km at 60 km/h, back at 80 km/h. Average speed? (K3)**  
   Understand: avg = total distance ÷ total time. Plan: find each time. Carry out: 4 h + 3 h = 7 h for 480 km → **≈ 68.6 km/h**. Look back: not 70, because more time is spent at the slower speed.
12. **Name the five stages of the computational process. Why test boundary cases? (K1/K2)**  
   Understand, plan, solve, verify, reflect. Errors cluster at boundaries (> instead of ≥); test at and around them.
13. **Attendance eligibility (40 classes, 75%): pseudocode + three tests. (K3)**  
   `INPUT attended; SET pct TO attended / 40 * 100; IF pct >= 75 THEN OUTPUT "Eligible" ELSE OUTPUT "Not eligible" ENDIF`. Tests: 30 (75%, eligible — boundary), 29 (72.5%, not), 40 (100%, eligible).
14. **Name four of Norman's principles; affordance vs signifier; evaluate an ATM. (K1–K3)**  
   Affordance, signifier, feedback, mapping, constraints, consistency. A door *affords* pushing; the "Pull" sign is the *signifier*. ATM: feedback (beeps, progress), constraints (card fits one way), signifiers (buttons beside options); improve with a language choice at the start.
15. **Four quadrants; why ask about past experiences; rewrite "Would you use a library booking app?". (K1–K3)**  
   Says, thinks, does, feels. People predict their future badly and are polite; real past events give honest detail. "Tell me about the last time you looked for a library seat." "What did you do when you couldn't find one?"
16. **POV structure; solution-smuggling; POV + 2 HMW for exam study space. (K1–K3)**  
   [User] needs [need] because [insight]. Putting a solution in the problem statement closes off better options. "A hostel student needs quiet evening study space during exams because her room is noisy and the library closes at 8 PM." HMW provide quiet space after 8 PM? HMW make shared rooms quieter in exam weeks?
17. **Functional vs non-functional; why testable; user story for library seat booking. (K1–K3)**  
   Functional = what it does (book a seat); non-functional = how well (500 simultaneous users). Testable so everyone agrees whether it's met. "As a student, I want to book a library seat for two hours so that I have a guaranteed place to study" — 1-hour slots up to 2 h; released if not checked in within 15 min; instant confirmation.

notes.title: CDT Unit 2 — ma'am's check-your-understanding questions
notes.content:
From the end of each chapter of ma'am's Unit II course notes (`course-notes/Unit_2_Notes_CDT.pdf`), with her model answers condensed. Her practice questions are the best guide to her exam.

1. **Name the four measures of creative output. (K1)**  
   Fluency, flexibility, originality, elaboration.
2. **Why must an idea be both novel and useful? (K2)**  
   Novelty without usefulness solves nothing; usefulness without novelty only repeats what exists.
3. **Core rules of divergent and convergent thinking; premature convergence. (K1/K2)**  
   No criticism during generation; no new ideas during evaluation. Premature convergence = settling on the obvious too early because ideas were judged as spoken; prevent by separating modes in time and naming the mode.
4. **A team skips the first diamond. Consequence? (K4)**  
   A good solution to the wrong problem — the problem was assumed, not explored and verified with users.
5. **Osborn's rules; production blocking and evaluation apprehension. (K1/K2)**  
   Defer judgement, quantity, wild ideas, combine and improve. Only one person speaks at a time so others forget ideas; fear of judgement stops bold ideas.
6. **Run the first ten minutes of a brainstorm on hostel food waste. (K3)**  
   Write the HMW on the board; explain the four rules and a target (30 ideas in 15 min); everyone writes three ideas silently; go round capturing every idea and stopping criticism.
7. **What do 6, 3, 5 stand for? A 4-3-5 variant with 4 rounds? (K1/K3)**  
   6 participants, 3 ideas each per round, 5 minutes per round. 4-3-5: 4 × 3 × 4 = **48 ideas in 20 minutes**.
8. **Expand SCAMPER; Adapt vs Modify; Eliminate + Reverse for the hostel mess. (K1–K3)**  
   Substitute, Combine, Adapt, Modify, Put to another use, Eliminate, Reverse. Adapt borrows from another context (fitness streaks); Modify changes an attribute (5-second check-in). Eliminate the queue with pre-selected portions; Reverse with a live "least crowded now" indicator.
9. **Five steps of a mind map; why one keyword per branch? (K1/K2)**  
   Centre, main branches, sub-branches, colour and images, review later. One word triggers more associations and keeps the map uncluttered.
10. **Who coined lateral thinking and when? Vertical vs lateral. (K1/K2)**  
   Edward de Bono, 1967. Vertical: logical, sequential, each step correct, deepens one approach. Lateral: sideways to new approaches, tolerates wrong steps, values movement over judgement.
11. **Five DT stages; why ask about the last time; rewrite "Students need a better canteen app". (K1–K3)**  
   Empathize, define, ideate, prototype, test. A specific recent event is remembered accurately. POV: "A student with a 20-minute lunch break needs food quickly because the queue takes longer than the break." HMW make sure students with short breaks eat on time?
12. **Impact–effort quadrants; why silent dot voting; weighted total 7/6/8/5 at 0.4/0.3/0.2/0.1; 7.5 vs 7.1. (K1–K4)**  
   Quick wins, big bets, fill-ins, money pit. Silent so nobody anchors on others. 2.8 + 1.8 + 1.6 + 0.5 = **6.7**. Too close to decide: examine which criteria separate them, check scores with evidence, or prototype both and test.

notes.title: CDT Unit 3 — ma'am's check-your-understanding questions
notes.content:
From the end of each chapter of ma'am's Unit III course notes (`course-notes/Unit_3_Notes_CDT.pdf`), with her model answers condensed. Her practice questions are the best guide to her exam.

1. **Define an algorithm; algorithm vs program; area of a rectangle. (K1–K3)**  
   A finite sequence of well-defined instructions: input → process → output. Algorithm = logical steps, language-independent; program = written in a language for a computer. Input length, breadth; area ← length × breadth; output area.
2. **Five essentials; finiteness vs effectiveness; "keep dividing by 2". (K1–K4)**  
   Input, output, definiteness, finiteness, effectiveness. Finiteness: stops; effectiveness: each step can be done. Violates finiteness and output → while N > 1, divide by 2 and count; output the count.
3. **Two advantages of pseudocode; what is a trace; Celsius → Fahrenheit for 25. (K1–K3)**  
   Language-independent; logic without syntax; easy to review. A trace follows the algorithm by hand recording each variable. F = 25 × 9/5 + 32 = **77**.
4. **Symbols for decision, I/O, start/end; flowchart vs pseudocode use; larger of two. (K1–K3)**  
   Diamond; parallelogram; rounded rectangle. Flowchart for non-programmers (admission procedure); pseudocode for long, changing algorithms. Start → Input A, B → A > B? → Yes print A / No print B → End.
5. **Define decomposition and pattern recognition; 5, 10, 15, 20 …; plan a class trip. (K1–K3)**  
   Breaking into sub-problems; spotting similarities to reuse a solution. Rule 5n, 10th term **50**. Destination & permission · transport · budget & collection · schedule & safety.
6. **True AND False, True OR False, NOT False; positive/negative/zero; marks > 40 bug. (K1–K4)**  
   False, True, True. `IF n > 0 … ELSE IF n < 0 … ELSE "Zero"`. Exactly 40 fails because 40 > 40 is false — use >= (a boundary error).
7. **Four parts of a loop; WHILE vs FOR; even numbers 2–20; the i + 1 bug. (K1–K4)**  
   Initialise, condition, body, update. WHILE when repetitions depend on a condition (read until 0). `FOR i FROM 1 TO 10 DO OUTPUT 2 * i ENDFOR`. i starts at 10 and increases, so i > 0 stays true: infinite — use i − 1.
8. **Expand LIFO/FIFO; dictionary for roll numbers; push A, B, pop, push C, D, pop. (K1–K3)**  
   Last In First Out = stack; First In First Out = queue. Unique keys give direct lookup. Remaining: **[A, C]**.
9. **What Big-O describes; why binary search needs sorting; Big-O of first/every/every pair; 1,024 items. (K1–K4)**  
   Growth of steps with input size, worst case, ignoring constants. It discards a half by comparing with the middle — only works if ordered. O(1), O(n), O(n²). Linear up to 1,024; binary ≈ 10 (2¹⁰ = 1024).

notes.title: CDT Unit 4 — ma'am's check-your-understanding questions
notes.content:
From the end of each chapter of ma'am's Unit IV course notes (`course-notes/Unit_4_Notes_CDT.pdf`), with her model answers condensed. Her practice questions are the best guide to her exam.

1. **Define critical thinking; sceptical vs cynical; "Exams postponed!" message. (K1–K3)**  
   Disciplined analysing, evaluating and reasoning to a well-justified conclusion. A sceptic accepts with evidence; a cynic rejects regardless. Ask the source; check the official website/notice; don't forward until verified; point the group to the official source.
2. **Eight elements; inference vs assumption; three standards on "Online classes are useless". (K1–K3)**  
   Purpose, question at issue, information, inferences, concepts, assumptions, implications, point of view. "The road is wet so it rained" (inference) assumes nobody washed it (assumption). Clarity: useless for what? Precision: all subjects? Accuracy: what evidence?
3. **Deductive vs inductive; valid vs sound; terms in the Neha syllogism; laptop argument. (K1–K4)**  
   General → certain specific; specific → probable general. Valid = follows by form; sound = valid + true premises. Major: study mathematics; minor: Neha; middle: engineer. Invalid — affirming the consequent.
4. **Gate that's 1 when inputs differ; why NAND/NOR universal; Y = (A AND B) OR (NOT A). (K1–K3)**  
   XOR. Any gate and so any circuit can be built from only NAND (or only NOR). 00→1, 01→1, 10→0, 11→1.
5. **A : B :: C : D meaning; why order matters; Pen : Write :: Knife : ?; 4 : 16 :: 6 : ?; Author : Book :: Programmer : ? (K1–K3)**  
   A relates to B as C to D. Relationships have direction. Cut · **36** (square) · program / software.
6. **Four checks for causation; correlation vs causation example; 5 Whys on a failed demo. (K1–K3)**  
   Order, consistency, mechanism, alternatives ruled out. Front-row students score higher, but motivation drives both (confounder). Crashed → no DB connection → password changed → cloud account reset → nobody documented credentials or tested setup → root cause: **no deployment checklist**.
7. **"Support this policy or you don't care"; fallacy vs bias; sunk-cost app; grandfather smoked to 95. (K1–K4)**  
   False dilemma. Fallacy = error in an argument's structure; bias = systematic tendency in a person's judgement. Sunk cost — decide on future costs and benefits with stop criteria agreed in advance. Hasty generalisation from one anecdote (+ availability bias).
8. **Expand CRAAP; why experiments beat testimonials; CRAAP on a "guaranteed" exam-cracking video. (K1–K3)**  
   Currency, relevance, authority, accuracy, purpose. Controlled comparison attributes the effect to the factor; a testimonial is one biased case. Current pattern? your exam? presenter's verifiable results? "guaranteed" backed by data? purpose — probably selling a course.
9. **Risk vs uncertainty; maximin choice; EV at P(high) = 0.6; why people choose differently. (K1–K4)**  
   Under risk probabilities are known (EV); under uncertainty they aren't (criteria). **B** — its worst (5) is the best worst. EV(A) = 36, EV(B) = 26 → A. Different attitudes to risk, ability to absorb losses, probability estimates.

notes.title: CDT Unit 5 — ma'am's check-your-understanding questions
notes.content:
From the end of each chapter of ma'am's Unit V course notes (`course-notes/Unit_5_Notes_CDT.pdf`), with her model answers condensed. Her practice questions are the best guide to her exam.

1. **Four pillars; abstraction in a navigation app; all four pillars. (K1–K4)**  
   Decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction, algorithms. Roads → graph of nodes and weighted edges, other details ignored. Components (maps, traffic, routing, guidance, ETA) · graph · congestion patterns · Dijkstra's or A*.
2. **Define abstraction; why no exact distances on a metro map; abstract a train for booking vs maintenance. (K1–K3)**  
   Removing unnecessary detail to focus on what matters. Passengers need order of stations and changes, not geography. Booking: number, route, stations, timings, classes, seats. Maintenance: coach IDs, mileage, condition, fault history.
3. **Food delivery subsystems; fraud alert as inductive; a canteen pattern. (K1–K3)**  
   Customer app, restaurant side, delivery partner, payments. Based on past behaviour — likely, not certain — so verify. Demand per dish by weekday (fewer lunches on Saturdays) to adjust quantities.
4. **Complexity of driver matching; why best_dist = infinity; only rating ≥ 4. (K1–K3)**  
   O(n). So the first free driver is always closer and becomes the first best. `IF d.free AND d.rating >= 4 AND dist(d) < best_dist THEN`.
5. **Define a prototype; compare fidelities; prototype for a timetable voice assistant. (K1–K3)**  
   Quick, cheap, early version built to learn. Low paper sketches (minutes) · medium Figma wireframe (hours) · high coded app (weeks). **Wizard of Oz** — a person answers behind the scenes first.
6. **Lean Startup stages; Build–Measure–Learn and short loops; why A/B changes one thing. (K1–K3)**  
   Build, measure, learn. Smallest test → real behaviour → keep/pivot/drop; short loops find wrong ideas cheaply. So the difference can be attributed to that one change.
7. **Four privacy-by-design principles; how algorithms become biased; face-recognition risks. (K1–K4)**  
   Data minimisation, consent, purpose limitation, security. Trained on historical data reflecting past unfairness. Privacy — encrypted templates, delete after semester, attendance only, opt-out. Bias — test accuracy across groups, manual fallback.
8. **IDEO's three lenses; incremental vs disruptive; UVP + metrics for a textbook exchange. (K1–K3)**  
   Desirable, feasible, viable. Faster charger vs digital payments replacing cash. "Buy last year's books at half price from seniors on your campus"; books listed/exchanged per month, % sold within two weeks.
9. **How many SDGs and by when; pattern recognition in canteen waste; an SDG solution. (K1–K3)**  
   17, adopted 2015, target 2030. Weekly demand patterns per dish let the kitchen forecast portions. SDG 6 leaking taps: decompose by block/floor, abstract taps to flow readings, night-flow pattern, IF 1–5 AM flow > threshold THEN alert; prototype with manual readings; compare water use.
